title: Acute Ischemic Stroke & TIA: Time-Critical Nursing Care
html:
Acute ischemic stroke is interrupted blood flow to part of the brain; every delay may increase permanent disability. A transient ischemic attack (TIA) causes temporary focal neurologic symptoms but is also an emergency warning of future stroke. The RN supports rapid recognition, a precise last-known-well history, imaging and treatment readiness, repeated neurologic assessment, and prevention of secondary harm. A bedside exam cannot safely distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke; urgent imaging and the stroke team's assessment guide treatment.

Learning goals

  • Recognize sudden focal neurologic deficits, including posterior-circulation findings, and record last known well accurately.
  • Explain why glucose testing and urgent brain imaging precede stroke-specific treatment decisions.
  • Prepare for clinician-selected IV thrombolysis or endovascular thrombectomy without treating the time window as the only eligibility criterion.
  • Monitor for neurologic decline, bleeding, aspiration, fever, glucose problems, and functional needs.
  • Describe why resolved TIA symptoms still require urgent evaluation and a cause-specific prevention plan.

Recognize stroke and establish the timeline

Use a rapid screen such as BE-FAST: sudden Balance difficulty, Eye or vision change, Facial droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. Also watch for unilateral numbness, new neglect, aphasia, severe gait or coordination change, or abrupt unexplained altered consciousness. Posterior-circulation stroke may feature vertigo with other neurologic signs, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, or weakness; do not dismiss these as simple dizziness. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, vital signs, and capillary glucose while activating the stroke response. Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and should be identified promptly, but a corrected glucose does not cancel assessment of persistent focal deficits.

Last known well means the last time the patient was observed at neurologic baseline, not when the deficit was discovered. Ask the patient and witnesses about onset, sleep and wake times, prior function, and changes during transport; document who provided the history and any uncertainty. A wake-up stroke has a last-known-well time before sleep unless further evidence clarifies it. Record anticoagulants or antiplatelets, last doses, recent surgery or bleeding, previous stroke, seizure, and major comorbidities without delaying urgent imaging. Use an objective baseline neurologic exam and a standardized scale such as NIHSS under local protocol, including pupils, gaze, visual fields, face, limbs, sensation, language, speech, and attention. A low NIHSS score can still hide a disabling deficit.

Imaging separates treatment pathways

Noncontrast head CT or another emergency brain-imaging pathway is used rapidly to identify hemorrhage and guide acute decisions. Vascular imaging can reveal a large-vessel occlusion, and selected patients need advanced imaging to assess salvageable tissue. The stroke team decides the imaging sequence; avoid delaying a time-sensitive therapy with nonessential tasks. Do not give aspirin, anticoagulants, or thrombolytics simply because a patient has stroke-like symptoms before hemorrhage is excluded and the authorized treatment plan is clear. If hemorrhage is found, management changes substantially; this course covers hemorrhagic stroke in a later lesson.

Reperfusion: eligibility is individualized

For eligible adults with disabling acute ischemic stroke, current AHA/ASA guidance supports IV alteplase or tenecteplase within the standard 4.5-hour window; selected patients may qualify beyond that window using advanced imaging criteria. The team evaluates imaging, contraindications, blood pressure, bleeding risk, and the actual deficit—not a clock alone. An isolated non-disabling deficit may have a different antiplatelet pathway instead of IV thrombolysis. Do not independently decide eligibility or administer an antithrombotic before the team confirms the pathway.

Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) can restore flow in selected large-vessel occlusions, sometimes beyond the IV thrombolysis window, based on vessel, imaging, time, and clinical features. A possible EVT candidate should be routed to an appropriate stroke-capable service without assuming that lack of IV thrombolysis eligibility ends treatment options. Prepare IV access, ordered blood work and imaging, medication history, transfer information, and communication with the stroke and neurointerventional teams. After IV thrombolysis or EVT, follow the service's neurologic, blood-pressure, access-site, and bleeding surveillance schedule. New severe headache, vomiting, acute blood-pressure change, new neurologic deficit, or reduced consciousness requires immediate escalation for possible intracranial hemorrhage or other complication. Do not apply an unqualified rule to drive systolic pressure below 140 mm Hg after reperfusion; targets are treatment- and patient-specific.

Protect brain, airway, and function after the hyperacute phase

Continue serial neurologic and perfusion assessments, watch cardiac rhythm and oxygenation, monitor fever and glucose, and communicate any change from baseline. Avoid hypoglycemia; intensive glucose lowering to 80–130 mg/dL is not recommended solely to improve ischemic-stroke outcome. Maintain prescribed blood-pressure parameters rather than reflexively lowering every elevated value, because goals vary with reperfusion status and comorbidity. Position and mobilize according to neurologic stability and the interdisciplinary plan, and prevent pressure injury, falls, venous thromboembolism, and urinary complications.

Keep the patient nothing by mouth, including oral medication and water, until a trained professional completes a validated swallowing screen. If the screen is failed, follow the plan for speech-language pathology assessment and an alternative route for essential medications and nutrition. Oral hygiene and aspiration precautions matter even when the patient is not eating. Assess communication, cognition, visual neglect, mood, mobility, activities of daily living, and caregiver needs. Explain actions to the patient even when speech output is impaired; aphasia does not automatically mean loss of understanding. Early rehabilitation and discharge planning involve PT, OT, speech-language pathology, case management, the patient, and family or support people.

TIA and prevention: disappearance is not reassurance

A TIA is not a reason to wait for routine follow-up. Even when symptoms resolve, the patient needs urgent evaluation for brain and vascular disease, atrial fibrillation or other cardiac source, and treatable risk factors. Imaging may reveal an infarction despite apparent recovery, changing the diagnosis and plan. Secondary prevention depends on the cause: antiplatelet therapy is common for noncardioembolic disease; anticoagulation is generally considered for atrial fibrillation when appropriate; short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is reserved for selected patients, not all strokes and not indefinitely. The authorized team selects treatment and timing after weighing bleeding and infarct characteristics. Teach the patient to call emergency services for new or recurrent symptoms rather than driving or waiting to see whether they disappear. Support individualized blood-pressure, lipid, diabetes, smoking, physical-activity, medication-adherence, and follow-up plans.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify sudden focal deficits, airway and glucose abnormalities, last known well, and deviations from neurologic baseline.
  2. Analyze cues: Consider stroke versus mimic, but remember that symptoms alone cannot distinguish ischemia from hemorrhage; correlate imaging and treatment history.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Threatened airway, rapidly progressing deficit, possible large-vessel occlusion, and post-treatment hemorrhage outrank routine tasks.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate the stroke pathway, prepare urgent brain and vascular imaging, gather time and medication history, and anticipate selected reperfusion options.
  5. Take action: Support ordered treatment and protocol-based monitoring, protect swallowing and skin, and coordinate communication, rehabilitation, and prevention.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Compare serial neurologic findings, vital signs, bleeding and aspiration signs, functional goals, and understanding of the emergency and prevention plan.

Clinical example

At 08:10, a family member finds a client with new left-sided weakness and slurred speech. The client was last seen normal at 06:30, before returning to sleep; 08:10 is the discovery time, not last known well. The RN activates the stroke response, checks airway and glucose, records the witness's history and medication list, establishes a baseline neurologic assessment, and prepares for immediate imaging. Even if weakness starts to improve, the RN continues the emergency pathway because TIA or evolving stroke remains possible.

Original educational synthesis. Stroke recognition, imaging, medication selection and timing, reperfusion, blood-pressure targets, and post-treatment monitoring require current patient data, authorized orders, local stroke protocols, specialist decisions, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official AHA/ASA product.
